extracted.intended_audience: authors/implementers creating or encoding Content MathML (web developers, MathML tool and renderer implementers)
extracted.subtask_description: Reference/specification describing the syntax, schema class, semantics, and example usage for MathML operator and constructor elements (n-ary, binary, unary operators; set/matrix/list constructors; statistical and linear-algebra operators). Intended to guide correct encoding and interpretation of MathML Content markup.

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary Logical Operators (<and/>, <or/>, <xor/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: These elements represent n-ary functions taking Boolean arguments and returning a Boolean value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments may be explicitly specified in the enclosing apply element, or specified via qualifier elements. and is true if all arguments are true, and false otherwise. or is true if any of the arguments are true, and false otherwise. xor is the logical exclusive or function: it is true if there are an odd number of true arguments or false otherwise. Examples (Content MathML and Strict Content MathML) and sample presentation (a ∧ b, ⋀i=0ⁿ(a_i>0)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selector (<selector/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selector element is the operator for indexing into vectors, matrices and lists. It accepts one or more arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First argument identifies the vector/matrix/list; subsequent arguments indicate selection. With a single argument, selector gives the sequence of all elements (ordering for a matrix: first by column then by row — entries listed first a1,1,a1,2,...,a2,1,a2,2,...). With two arguments: if first is vector/list, second specifies index; if first is matrix, second specifies index of a matrix row. With three arguments: last is ignored for list/vector; for matrix, second and third specify row and column indices. Examples and sample presentations provided (V1, matrix indexing).

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary Set Operators (<union/>, <intersect/>, <cartesianproduct/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators for n-ary set operations: union, intersect, and cartesianproduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: union denotes the set containing all elements that occur in any of its argument sets. intersect denotes the set containing elements that occur in all argument sets. cartesianproduct represents the Cartesian product operator. Arguments may be explicitly specified in apply or via qualifier elements. Examples and sample presentations (A ∪ B, A ∩ B ∩ C, A × B). Qualifier examples show domain-of-application usage (⋃_L S, ⋂_L S).

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary Matrix Constructors (<vector/>, <matrix/>, <matrixrow/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructor elements to build vectors and matrices: vector is ordered n-tuple; matrix is made up of matrixrow children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vectors are regarded as equivalent to a single-column matrix; transpose of a vector as single-row matrix. Components may be given explicitly or specified by rule (see container-markup for constructor symbols). Matrix entries may be given explicitly or computed by providing a function and a 2-dimensional domain; matrixrow entries are not directly rendered outside context of matrix. Examples show explicit vectors and matrices and rule-specified matrices (entries being i^j over domains). Note: behavior differs substantially from presentation elements mtable/mtr.

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary Set-Theoretic Constructors (<set>, <list>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructors for mathematical sets and lists from arguments; set takes attribute type (set or multiset), list takes order attribute (numeric or lexicographic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members may be explicit children or specified by rule (function + domain). No implied ordering for sets. Lists have explicit order; ordering may be unspecified when produced by rule so order attribute can be set to 'numeric' or 'lexicographic'. Examples include explicit element lists and rule/condition-specified sets/lists, and sample presentations ({a,b,c}, (a,b,c)). Examples show set-builder and domain-of-application forms and the need to indicate ordering for lists constructed by rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary Arithmetic Relations (<eq/>, <gt/>, <lt/>, <geq/>, <leq/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements represent equality and ordering relations that return true or false depending on relationship of arguments (allow transitive chains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MathML allows transitive relations used with multiple arguments (e.g., a<b<c<d). Underlying Strict Content MathML symbols are classed as binary, so predicate_on_list is used to express n-ary semantics (essentially conjunction of the binary predicate applied pairwise). eq, gt, lt, geq, leq represent equality, greater-than, less-than, greater-or-equal, less-or-equal respectively. Examples include chaining (x = 2/4 = 1/2) and other sample presentations (4 ≥ 3 ≥ 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary Set-Theoretic Relations (<subset/>, <prsubset/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements represent subset and proper-subset relations and may be used as n-ary operators to express chains (each argument subset of predecessor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although underlying symbols are binary in Strict Content MathML, predicate_on_list semantics allow n-ary chaining (e.g. A ⊂ B ⊂ C). Examples and sample presentations provided (A ⊆ B, A ⊂ B ⊂ C).

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary/Unary Arithmetic Operators (<min/>, <max/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: min and max may be used as n-ary functions; when given a single argument, special interpretation applies — function applied to elements represented by that argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underlying symbol in Strict Content MathML is Unary; when used with 0 or more than 1 argument, the function is applied to the set constructed from the explicitly supplied arguments per the rule. min returns smallest of arguments; max returns largest. When applied to infinite sets, minimal or maximal argument may not exist. Arguments may be explicit or specified via qualifier elements. Examples include min{a,b}, max{2,3,5}, min applied to set-comprehension forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary/Unary Statistical Operators (<mean/>, <median/>, <mode/>, <sdev/>, <variance/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical elements that represent common summary statistics; special interpretation when a single argument is supplied (applied to elements represented by that argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: mean returns arithmetic mean/average of a data set or random variable. median returns a number separating lower half from upper half. mode denotes the most frequent value. sdev denotes standard deviation (square root of variance). variance represents variance (average squared deviations). Underlying symbol in Strict Content MathML is Unary; examples include explicit lists and variable arguments (⟨3,4,3,7,4⟩, ⟨X⟩ or X̄), sdev(X), σ(X), σ²(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary Operators (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary operators take two arguments and map to OpenMath symbols via Rewrite: element without special rewrite rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binary constructor interval is similar but uses constructor syntax where arguments are children and symbol depends on type attribute (see Interval). This general rule applies across binary operator classes described below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary Arithmetic Operators (<quotient/>, <divide/>, <minus/>, <power/>, <rem/>, <root/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary arithmetic elements representing integer quotient, division in number field, subtraction (or unary minus), exponentiation, remainder (modulus), and root extraction (nth root).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: quotient: integer division semantics — q such that a = b*q + r with |r| < |b| and a*r positive; q called quotient and r remainder. divide: division in a number field. minus: usable as unary (−x) or binary (x−y). power: first argument raised to second. rem: modulus returning remainder r such that a = b*q + r with |r| < |b| and a*r positive. root: degree element (second child of apply) specifies degree (default 2 if absent) — square roots degree=2, cube roots degree=3. Examples and sample presentations (⌊a/b⌋, a/b, x−y, x^3, a mod b, mroot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary Logical Operators (<implies/>, <equivalent/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical implication and logical equivalence operators taking two Boolean expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: implies evaluates to false only when first argument is true and second is false; otherwise true. equivalent asserts two Boolean expressions are logically equivalent (same Boolean value for any inputs). Examples (A ⇒ B, a ≡ ¬¬a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary Relations (<neq/>, <approx/>, <factorof/>, <tendsto/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary relation elements for inequality, approximate equality, factor relationship, and limiting (tends-to) relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: neq: not-equal relation, true unless two args equal. approx: asserts approximate equality. factorof: first argument is factor of second (true iff b mod a = 0). tendsto: expresses that a quantity tends to a specified value; used for limits and more general 'as x tends to y' statements. tendsto has attribute type to set direction of approach (common values include 'above' and 'below'). Examples and sample presentations provided (3 ≠ 4, π ≃ 22/7, a | b, x^2 → a^2 + ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary Linear Algebra Operators (<vectorproduct/>, <scalarproduct/>, <outerproduct/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators representing common vector/matrix products: vector (cross) product, scalar (dot) product, outer product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: vectorproduct: takes two three-dimensional vector arguments and returns a three-dimensional vector. scalarproduct: takes two vectors and returns scalar. outerproduct: takes two vectors and returns a matrix. Examples given show relationships (A×B = a b sin θ N, A·B = a b cos θ, A ⊗ B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary Set Operators (<in/>, <notin/>, <notsubset/>, <notprsubset/>, <setdiff/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set membership and negated relations plus set difference operator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: in: element ∈ set (two args: element, set). notin: element ∉ set. notsubset: first argument is not a subset of second. notprsubset: first argument is not a proper subset of second. setdiff: set difference — elements in first set but not in second. Examples and sample presentations provided (a ∈ A, a ∉ A, A ⊈ B, A ⊄ B, A ∖ B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unary Operators (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unary operators take a single argument and map to OpenMath symbols via Rewrite: element without need for special rewrite rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general class is followed by logical and arithmetic unary operator specifics (not, factorial, abs, conjugate, arg, real, imaginary, floor, ceiling, exp, minus, root).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unary Logical Operator (<not/>)
rubrics_metrics.description: not represents logical negation: takes one Boolean argument and returns the opposite Boolean value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: apply not to a yields ¬a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unary Arithmetic Operators (factorial, abs, conjugate, arg, real, imaginary, floor, ceiling, exp, minus, root)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various unary arithmetic operators with their mathematical semantics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: factorial: unary factorial on non-negative integers, n! = n×(n-1)×...×1. abs: absolute value (numerical value; modulus for complex argument). conjugate: complex conjugate. arg: angular argument (angle from positive real axis). real: real part of complex number. imaginary: imaginary part. floor: round down toward −∞ to nearest integer (takes real, returns integer). ceiling: round up toward +∞ (real→integer). exp: exponential function (inverse of ln). minus: can be unary (−x) or binary (x−y). root: treated as unary element with optional degree qualifier but represents nth-root operation (described earlier in binary arithmetic with degree qualifier). Examples and sample presentations provided (n!, |x|, complex conjugate notation, arg(x+iy), ℛ(x+iy), floor/ceiling examples, exp(x), unary minus example).
